condition: Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS) within 3 hours – Age Considerations
recommendation: For otherwise medically eligible patients ≥18 years old, IV alteplase within 3 hours is recommended equally for patients ≤80 or >80 years of age.
hint: Age alone should not exclude patients if the rest of the eligibility criteria are met.
original_text: For otherwise medically eligible patients ≥18 y of age, IV alteplase administration within 3 h is equally recommended for patients ≤80 and >80 y of age.† (COR I; LOE A)

condition: Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS) within 3 hours – Severe Stroke
recommendation: For patients presenting with severe stroke (e.g., significant NIHSS score), IV alteplase is indicated within 3 hours from symptom onset. Despite the increased risk of hemorrhagic transformation, clinical trials support continued benefit.
hint: Severe stroke should not be a standalone exclusion; weigh risk-benefit, but evidence supports potential functional gains.
original_text: For severe stroke, IV alteplase is indicated within 3 h from symptom onset of ischemic stroke. Despite increased risk of hemorrhagic transformation, there is still proven clinical benefit for patients with severe stroke symptoms.† (COR I; LOE A)

condition: Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS) within 3–4.5 hours – Age and Other Factors
recommendation: For patients ≤80 years of age without a history of both diabetes mellitus and prior stroke, with NIHSS score ≤25, not taking oral anticoagulants, and without large ischemic involvement (>1/3 MCA territory), IV alteplase is recommended in the 3 to 4.5-hour window.
hint: Patient selection is more stringent in the 3–4.5-hour window; carefully rule out large infarcts and other high-risk characteristics.
original_text: IV alteplase treatment in the 3- to 4.5-h time window is recommended for those patients ≤80 y of age, without a history of both diabetes mellitus and prior stroke, NIHSS score ≤25, not taking any OACs, and without imaging evidence of ischemic injury involving more than one-third of the MCA territory.† (COR I; LOE B-R)

condition: Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS) – Blood Glucose Considerations
recommendation: IV alteplase is recommended in otherwise eligible patients with an initial blood glucose level >50 mg/dL.
hint: Extremely low blood glucose (<50 mg/dL) can mimic stroke symptoms; confirm actual ischemic event before treatment.
original_text: IV alteplase is recommended in otherwise eligible patients with initial glucose levels >50 mg/dL.† (COR I; LOE A)

condition: Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS) – Neuroimaging (CT) Findings
recommendation: IV alteplase administration is recommended when NCCT shows early ischemic changes of only mild to moderate extent (excluding frank hypodensity).
hint: Subtle early changes on NCCT do not contraindicate alteplase use; extensive established hypodensity usually suggests large infarct risk.
original_text: IV alteplase administration is recommended in the setting of early ischemic changes on NCCT of mild to moderate extent (other than frank hypodensity).† (COR I; LOE A)

condition: AIS with prior antiplatelet monotherapy
recommendation: IV alteplase is recommended. The benefit of alteplase outweighs a possible small increased risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage.
original_text: “IV alteplase is recommended for patients taking antiplatelet drug monotherapy before stroke on the basis of evidence that the benefit of alteplase outweighs a possible small increased risk of sICH. (COR I; LOE A)”

condition: AIS with prior antiplatelet combination therapy
recommendation: IV alteplase is recommended. The benefit of alteplase outweighs a probable increased risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage.
original_text: “IV alteplase is recommended for patients taking antiplatelet drug combination therapy (eg, aspirin and clopidogrel) before stroke on the basis of evidence that the benefit of alteplase outweighs a probable increased risk of sICH. (COR I; LOE B-NR)”

condition: AIS with end-stage renal disease on dialysis
recommendation: IV alteplase is recommended if aPTT is normal.
hint: Elevated aPTT may increase hemorrhagic risk.
original_text: “In patients with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and normal aPTT, IV alteplase is recommended. (COR I; LOE C-LD) However, those with elevated aPTT may have elevated risk for hemorrhagic complications.”

condition: AIS for patients >80 years old in the 3–4.5h window
recommendation: IV alteplase is safe and can be as effective as in younger patients.
original_text: “For patients >80 y of age presenting in the 3- to 4.5-h window, IV alteplase is safe and can be as effective as in younger patients. (COR IIa; LOE B-NR)”

condition: AIS with prior stroke and diabetes mellitus in the 3–4.5h window
recommendation: IV alteplase may be as effective as in the 0–3h window and may be a reasonable option.
original_text: “In AIS patients with prior stroke and diabetes mellitus presenting in the 3- to 4.5-h window, IV alteplase may be as effective as treatment in the 0- to 3-h window and may be a reasonable option. (COR IIb; LOE B-NR)”

condition: AIS with severe stroke (NIHSS >25) in the 3–4.5h window
recommendation: The benefit of IV alteplase is uncertain for very severe stroke symptoms.
original_text: “The benefit of IV alteplase between 3 and 4.5 h from symptom onset for patients with very severe stroke symptoms (NIHSS score >25) is uncertain. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)”

condition: AIS with preexisting disability (mRS ≥2)
recommendation: IV alteplase may be reasonable, but decisions should consider quality of life, support, patient preferences, and goals of care.
original_text: “Preexisting disability does not seem to independently increase the risk of sICH after IV alteplase, but it may be associated with less neurological improvement and higher mortality. Therapy with IV alteplase may be reasonable. (COR IIb; LOE B-NR)”

condition: AIS with preexisting dementia
recommendation: IV alteplase may benefit patients with dementia. Individual considerations (life expectancy, function) are crucial.
original_text: “Patients with preexisting dementia may benefit from IV alteplase. Individual considerations such as life expectancy and premorbid level of function are important. (COR IIb; LOE B-NR)”

condition: AIS with moderate to severe stroke, early improvement but remaining deficits
recommendation: IV alteplase treatment is reasonable for patients who present with moderate to severe ischemic stroke and demonstrate early improvement but remain moderately impaired.
original_text: “IV alteplase treatment is reasonable for patients who present with moderate to severe ischemic stroke and demonstrate early improvement but remain moderately impaired. (COR IIa; LOE A)”

condition: AIS with seizure at onset
recommendation: IV alteplase is reasonable if residual impairments are due to stroke rather than postictal phenomenon.
original_text: “IV alteplase is reasonable in patients with a seizure at the time of onset of acute stroke if evidence suggests that residual impairments are secondary to stroke and not a postictal phenomenon. (COR IIa; LOE C-LD)”

condition: AIS with extreme blood glucose (<50 mg/dL or >400 mg/dL) normalized before treatment
recommendation: IV alteplase may be reasonable if patients are otherwise eligible.
original_text: “Treatment with IV alteplase in patients with AIS who present with initial glucose levels <50 or >400 mg/dL that are subsequently normalized and who are otherwise eligible may be reasonable. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)”

condition: AIS with warfarin use but INR ≤1.7 or PT <15s
recommendation: IV alteplase may be reasonable.
original_text: “IV alteplase may be reasonable in patients who have a history of warfarin use and an INR ≤1.7 or a PT <15 s. (COR IIb; LOE B-NR)”

condition: AIS with potential bleeding diathesis or coagulopathy (unknown status)
recommendation: IV alteplase may be considered on a case-by-case basis.
original_text: “The safety and efficacy of IV alteplase for acute stroke patients with a clinical history of potential bleeding diathesis or coagulopathy are unknown. IV alteplase may be considered on a case-by-case basis. (COR IIb; LOE C-EO)”

condition: AIS after recent lumbar dural puncture (within 7 days)
recommendation: IV alteplase may be considered.
original_text: “IV alteplase may be considered for patients who present with AIS, even in instances when they may have undergone a lumbar dural puncture in the preceding 7 d. (COR IIb; LOE C-EO)”

condition: AIS after an arterial puncture of a noncompressible vessel (within 7 days)
recommendation: Safety and efficacy of IV alteplase are uncertain.
original_text: “The safety and efficacy of administering IV alteplase to acute stroke patients who have had an arterial puncture of a noncompressible blood vessel in the 7 d preceding stroke symptoms are uncertain. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)”

condition: AIS with recent major trauma (within 14 days) not involving the head
recommendation: IV alteplase may be carefully considered, weighing risk of bleeding vs stroke severity.
original_text: “In AIS patients with recent major trauma (within 14 d) not involving the head, IV alteplase may be carefully considered, with the risks of bleeding from injuries weighed against the severity and potential disability from the ischemic stroke. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)”

condition: AIS with recent major surgery (within 14 days)
recommendation: IV alteplase may be considered for carefully selected patients, weighing increased risk of surgical-site hemorrhage.
original_text: “Use of IV alteplase in carefully selected patients presenting with AIS who have undergone a major surgery in the preceding 14 d may be considered, but the potential increased risk of surgical-site hemorrhage should be weighed against the anticipated benefits. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)”

condition: AIS with past gastrointestinal or genitourinary bleeding
recommendation: IV alteplase may be reasonable. However, administration within 21 days of a GI bleeding event is not recommended.
original_text: “Reported literature details a low bleeding risk with IV alteplase administration in the setting of past GI/genitourinary bleeding. Administration of IV alteplase in this patient population may be reasonable. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD) (Note: Alteplase administration within 21 d of a GI bleeding event is not recommended.)”

condition: Menstruation (no history of menorrhagia)
recommendation: IV alteplase is probably indicated in women who are menstruating who present with AIS and do not have a history of menorrhagia. However, women should be warned that alteplase treatment could increase the degree of menstrual flow.
hint: Inform the patient about possible increased menstrual flow; otherwise, no further restriction if no menorrhagia history.
original_text: IV alteplase is probably indicated in women who are menstruating who present with AIS and do not have a history of menorrhagia. However, women should be warned that alteplase treatment could increase the degree of menstrual flow. (COR IIa; LOE C-EO)

condition: Menstruation with recent or active vaginal bleeding causing clinically significant anemia
recommendation: When there is a history of recent or active vaginal bleeding causing clinically significant anemia, then emergency consultation with a gynecologist is probably indicated before a decision about IV alteplase is made.
hint: Risk of exacerbating bleeding should be weighed against the benefits of thrombolysis; a gynecologist's input is advised.
original_text: When there is a history of recent or active vaginal bleeding causing clinically significant anemia, then emergency consultation with a gynecologist is probably indicated before a decision about IV alteplase is made. (COR IIa; LOE C-EO)

condition: Menorrhagia without clinically significant anemia or hypotension
recommendation: Because the potential benefits of IV alteplase probably outweigh the risks of serious bleeding in patients with recent or active history of menorrhagia without clinically significant anemia or hypotension, IV alteplase administration may be considered.
hint: Carefully assess risk-benefit; bleeding risk may increase, but potential benefit often outweighs risk.
original_text: Because the potential benefits of IV alteplase probably outweigh the risks of serious bleeding in patients with recent or active history of menorrhagia without clinically significant anemia or hypotension, IV alteplase administration may be considered. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Extracranial cervical arterial dissection
recommendation: IV alteplase in AIS known or suspected to be associated with extracranial cervical arterial dissection is reasonably safe within 4.5 hours and probably recommended.
hint: No substantial increase in hemorrhagic complications for extracranial dissection has been shown; consider standard 4.5-hour window.
original_text: IV alteplase in AIS known or suspected to be associated with extracranial cervical arterial dissection is reasonably safe within 4.5 h and probably recommended. (COR IIa; LOE C-LD)

condition: Intracranial arterial dissection
recommendation: The usefulness and hemorrhagic risk of IV alteplase in AIS known or suspected to be associated with intracranial arterial dissection are unknown and not well established.
hint: Evidence is limited; clinicians should weigh potential hemorrhagic risk against possible benefit.
original_text: IV alteplase usefulness and hemorrhagic risk in AIS known or suspected to be associated with intracranial arterial dissection remain unknown, uncertain and not well established. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Unruptured intracranial aneurysm (<10 mm)
recommendation: For patients presenting with AIS who are known to harbor a small or moderate-sized (<10 mm) unruptured and unsecured intracranial aneurysm, administration of IV alteplase is reasonable and probably recommended.
hint: Small or moderate aneurysms generally do not significantly increase hemorrhagic risk; treatment can proceed.
original_text: For patients presenting with AIS who are known to harbor a small or moderate-sized (<10 mm) unruptured and unsecured intracranial aneurysm, administration of IV alteplase is reasonable and probably recommended. (COR IIa; LOE C-LD)

condition: Giant unruptured, unsecured intracranial aneurysm (≥10 mm)
recommendation: Usefulness and risk of IV alteplase in patients with AIS who harbor a giant unruptured and unsecured intracranial aneurysm are not well established.
hint: Careful risk-benefit analysis is crucial; hemorrhage risks may be higher for giant aneurysms.
original_text: Usefulness and risk of IV alteplase in patients with AIS who harbor a giant unruptured and unsecured intracranial aneurysm are not well established. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Intracranial vascular malformations (unruptured, untreated)
recommendation: For patients presenting with AIS who are known to harbor an unruptured and untreated intracranial vascular malformation, the usefulness and risks of administration of IV alteplase are not well established.
hint: Hemorrhage risk is uncertain; thorough assessment is needed if the vascular malformation is discovered.
original_text: For patients presenting with AIS who are known to harbor an unruptured and untreated intracranial vascular malformation the usefulness and risks of administration of IV alteplase are not well established. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Intracranial vascular malformations with severe stroke deficits
recommendation: Because of the increased risk of ICH in this population, IV alteplase may be considered in patients with stroke with severe neurological deficits and a high likelihood of morbidity and mortality to outweigh the anticipated risk of ICH.
hint: In life-threatening or severely disabling stroke, the benefit of thrombolysis may outweigh the increased bleeding risk.
original_text: Because of the increased risk of ICH in this population of patients, IV alteplase may be considered in patients with stroke with severe neurological deficits and a high likelihood of morbidity and mortality to outweigh the anticipated risk of ICH. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) 1–10
recommendation: In otherwise eligible patients who have previously had a small number (1–10) of CMBs demonstrated on MRI, administration of IV alteplase is reasonable.
hint: Presence of few CMBs does not preclude treatment, but counsel on potential hemorrhagic risk.
original_text: In otherwise eligible patients who have previously had a small number (1–10) of CMBs demonstrated on MRI, administration of IV alteplase is reasonable. (COR IIa; Level B-NR)

condition: Cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) >10
recommendation: In otherwise eligible patients who have previously had a high burden of CMBs (>10) demonstrated on MRI, treatment with IV alteplase may be associated with an increased risk of sICH, and the benefits are uncertain. Treatment may be reasonable if there is potential for substantial benefit.
hint: Heavier CMB burden raises caution; however, with a large potential neurological recovery, thrombolysis may still be reasonable.
original_text: In otherwise eligible patients who have previously had a high burden of CMBs (>10) demonstrated on MRI, treatment with IV alteplase may be associated with an increased risk of sICH, and the benefits of treatment are uncertain. Treatment may be reasonable if there is the potential for substantial benefit. (COR IIb; Level B-NR)

condition: Concomitant tirofiban or eptifibatide use
recommendation: The efficacy of the IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors tirofiban and eptifibatide coadministered with IV alteplase is not well established.
hint: Limited data on safety/efficacy when combining IV alteplase with glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors.
original_text: The efficacy of the IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors tirofiban and eptifibatide coadministered with IV alteplase is not well established. (COR IIb; Level B-NR)

condition: Extra-axial intracranial neoplasms
recommendation: IV alteplase treatment is probably recommended for patients with AIS who harbor an extra-axial intracranial neoplasm.
hint: Extra-axial tumors (e.g., meningioma) generally pose less risk of intracranial hemorrhage than intra-axial lesions, so thrombolysis can be considered.
original_text: IV alteplase treatment is probably recommended for patients with AIS who harbor an extra-axial intracranial neoplasm. (COR IIa; LOE C-EO)

condition: Concurrent AIS and acute MI
recommendation: For patients presenting with concurrent AIS and acute MI, treatment with IV alteplase at the dose appropriate for cerebral ischemia, followed by percutaneous coronary angioplasty and stenting if indicated, is reasonable.
hint: Stroke protocol dosing applies first; coronary intervention can follow as needed.
original_text: For patients presenting with concurrent AIS and acute MI, treatment with IV alteplase at the dose appropriate for cerebral ischemia, followed by percutaneous coronary angioplasty and stenting if indicated, is reasonable. (COR IIa; LOE C-EO)

condition: Recent MI (non-STEMI within past 3 months)
recommendation: For patients presenting with AIS and a history of recent MI in the past 3 months, treating the ischemic stroke with IV alteplase is reasonable if the recent MI was non-STEMI.
hint: Non-STEMI type is generally associated with lower risk of cardiac wall rupture post-thrombolysis.
original_text: For patients presenting with AIS and a history of recent MI in the past 3 mo, treating the ischemic stroke with IV alteplase is reasonable if the recent MI was non-STEMI. (COR IIa; LOE C-LD)

condition: Recent MI (STEMI right or inferior myocardium within past 3 months)
recommendation: For patients presenting with AIS and a history of recent MI in the past 3 months, treating the ischemic stroke with IV alteplase is reasonable if the recent MI was a STEMI involving the right or inferior myocardium.
hint: Right or inferior STEMI typically carries reduced risk of myocardial rupture compared with anterior STEMI.
original_text: For patients presenting with AIS and a history of recent MI in the past 3 mo, treating the ischemic stroke with IV alteplase is reasonable if the recent MI was a STEMI involving the right or inferior myocardium. (COR IIa; LOE C-LD)

condition: Recent MI (STEMI left anterior myocardium within past 3 months)
recommendation: For patients presenting with AIS and a history of recent MI in the past 3 months, treating the ischemic stroke with IV alteplase may be reasonable if the recent MI was a STEMI involving the left anterior myocardium.
hint: Higher caution for severe wall motion abnormalities and risk of cardiac rupture; individualized risk-benefit analysis is needed.
original_text: For patients presenting with AIS and a history of recent MI in the past 3 mo, treating the ischemic stroke with IV alteplase may be reasonable if the recent MI was a STEMI involving the left anterior myocardium. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Acute pericarditis with major AIS (likely severe disability)
recommendation: For patients with major AIS likely to produce severe disability and acute pericarditis, treatment with IV alteplase may be reasonable; urgent consultation with a cardiologist is recommended.
hint: Risk of hemopericardium should be weighed against stroke severity; cardiology input is critical.
original_text: For patients with major AIS likely to produce severe disability and acute pericarditis, treatment with IV alteplase may be reasonable (COR IIb; LOE C-EO); urgent consultation with a cardiologist is recommended.

condition: Acute pericarditis with moderate AIS (likely mild disability)
recommendation: For patients presenting with moderate AIS likely to produce mild disability and acute pericarditis, treatment with IV alteplase is of uncertain net benefit.
hint: Uncertain benefit may not justify increased risk of pericardial bleeding; carefully evaluate patient’s functional status and risk.
original_text: For patients presenting with moderate AIS likely to produce mild disability and acute pericarditis, treatment with IV alteplase is of uncertain net benefit. (COR IIb; LOE C-EO)

condition: Known left atrial or ventricular thrombus with major AIS (likely severe disability)
recommendation: For patients with major AIS likely to produce severe disability and known left atrial or ventricular thrombus, treatment with IV alteplase may be reasonable.
hint: Large intracardiac thrombi raise embolic and hemorrhagic complications; potential neurologic improvement may still justify therapy.
original_text: For patients with major AIS likely to produce severe disability and known left atrial or ventricular thrombus, treatment with IV alteplase may be reasonable. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Known left atrial or ventricular thrombus with moderate AIS (likely mild disability)
recommendation: For patients presenting with moderate AIS likely to produce mild disability and known left atrial or ventricular thrombus, treatment with IV alteplase is of uncertain net benefit.
hint: Smaller stroke deficits reduce the urgency for high-risk thrombolysis; weigh carefully the risk of systemic embolization or hemorrhage.
original_text: For patients presenting with moderate AIS likely to produce mild disability and known left atrial or ventricular thrombus, treatment with IV alteplase is of uncertain net benefit. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Cardiac myxoma with major AIS (likely severe disability)
recommendation: For patients with major AIS likely to produce severe disability and cardiac myxoma, treatment with IV alteplase may be reasonable.
hint: Risk remains poorly characterized; large tumor fragments could dislodge, but major stroke severity may prompt IV alteplase consideration.
original_text: For patients with major AIS likely to produce severe disability and cardiac myxoma, treatment with IV alteplase may be reasonable. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Papillary fibroelastoma with major AIS (likely severe disability)
recommendation: For patients presenting with major AIS likely to produce severe disability and papillary fibroelastoma, treatment with IV alteplase may be reasonable.
hint: Similar to myxoma, caution given potential for mass fragmentation; consider severity of stroke and potential benefits.
original_text: For patients presenting with major AIS likely to produce severe disability and papillary fibroelastoma, treatment with IV alteplase may be reasonable. (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)

condition: Procedural stroke (cardiac or cerebral angiographic complications)
recommendation: IV alteplase is reasonable for the treatment of AIS complications of cardiac or cerebral angiographic procedures, depending on the usual eligibility criteria.
hint: Treat procedural strokes following standard IV alteplase protocols if no other contraindications exist.
original_text: IV alteplase is reasonable for the treatment of AIS complications of cardiac or cerebral angiographic procedures, depending on the usual eligibility criteria. (COR IIa; LOE A)

condition: Systemic malignancy in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS)
recommendation: IV alteplase may be considered if the patient has a reasonable (>6 months) life expectancy and does not have other contraindications (such as significant coagulopathies, recent surgery, or active bleeding).
hint: Safety and efficacy are not well-established; use caution.
original_text: ‘The safety and efficacy of IV alteplase in patients with current malignancy are not well established.† (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)§ ... Patients with systemic malignancy and reasonable (>6 mo) life expectancy may benefit from IV alteplase if other contraindications do not coexist.’

condition: Pregnancy in patients with AIS
recommendation: IV alteplase may be considered for moderate or severe stroke during pregnancy when benefits of treatment outweigh risks (including uterine bleeding). The safety in the early postpartum period (<14 days) is not well established.
hint: Balance risk of hemorrhage versus the need for acute stroke treatment.
original_text: ‘IV alteplase administration may be considered in pregnancy when the anticipated benefits of treating moderate or severe stroke outweigh the anticipated increased risks of uterine bleeding.† (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)§ … The safety and efficacy of IV alteplase in the early postpartum period (<14 d after delivery) have not been well established.† (COR IIb; LOE C-LD)§’

condition: Ophthalmological conditions (e.g., hemorrhagic retinopathy)
recommendation: IV alteplase is reasonable in AIS patients with a history of hemorrhagic ophthalmic conditions, but the risk of additional visual loss must be weighed against potential neurologic benefit.
hint: Use caution if history of hemorrhagic retinopathy; individualized risk assessment is crucial.
original_text: ‘Use of IV alteplase in patients presenting with AIS who have a history of diabetic hemorrhagic retinopathy or other hemorrhagic ophthalmic conditions is reasonable … (COR IIa; LOE B-NR)§’

condition: Sickle cell disease in AIS
recommendation: IV alteplase can be beneficial for adults with known sickle cell disease who present with AIS and meet standard thrombolysis criteria.
hint: Presence of sickle cell alone does not rule out IV alteplase.
original_text: ‘IV alteplase for adults presenting with an AIS with known sickle cell disease can be beneficial. (COR IIa; LOE B-NR)‡’

condition: Hyperdense MCA sign on imaging
recommendation: IV alteplase can be beneficial in AIS patients with the hyperdense MCA sign if they meet standard eligibility criteria.
hint: A hyperdense MCA sign often indicates a significant clot burden, but does not itself preclude treatment.
original_text: ‘In patients with a hyperdense MCA sign, IV alteplase can be beneficial. (COR IIa; LOE B-NR)‡’

condition: Illicit drug use in AIS
recommendation: IV alteplase is reasonable when no other exclusions exist, but clinicians should be aware that illicit drug use may have contributed to the stroke.
hint: Rule out other contraindications before administering IV alteplase.
original_text: ‘…IV alteplase is reasonable in instances of illicit drug use–associated AIS in patients with no other exclusions.† (COR IIa; LOE C-LD)§’

condition: Stroke mimics (suspected AIS but uncertain diagnosis)
recommendation: Given low risk of symptomatic ICH in stroke mimics, initiating IV alteplase is likely preferable to delaying treatment for further diagnostic studies.
hint: Prompt treatment outweighs small hemorrhage risk if symptoms strongly suggest stroke.
original_text: ‘The risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage in the stroke mimic population is quite low; thus, starting IV alteplase is probably recommended … (COR IIa; LOE B-NR)§’

condition: Extensive hypoattenuation on CT (large core infarction)
recommendation: IV alteplase is not recommended for patients with extensive hypoattenuation (obvious hypodensity indicating irreversible injury). These patients generally have poor outcomes despite alteplase.
hint: Severe hypoattenuation usually represents large irreversible infarction, limiting efficacy and increasing risk.
original_text: ‘… administering IV alteplase to patients whose CT … exhibits extensive regions of clear hypoattenuation is not recommended … (COR III: No Benefit; LOE A)‖’

condition: Acute intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) on CT
recommendation: IV alteplase must not be administered if acute ICH is identified on imaging.
hint: Any sign of active intracranial bleeding is a strict contraindication to thrombolysis.
original_text: ‘IV alteplase should not be administered to a patient whose CT reveals an acute intracranial hemorrhage.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖’

condition: Prior ischemic stroke within 3 months
recommendation: Use of IV alteplase in patients with an AIS who have had an ischemic stroke within the past 3 months may be harmful.
hint: Increased risk of hemorrhage if prior recent stroke.
original_text: ‘Use of IV alteplase … who have had a prior ischemic stroke within 3 mo may be harmful.† (COR III: Harm; LOE B-NR)§‖’

condition: Severe head trauma within 3 months preceding AIS
recommendation: IV alteplase is contraindicated in AIS patients with recent severe head trauma (within 3 months).
hint: Risk of intracranial hemorrhage is elevated after recent serious head injury.
original_text: ‘In AIS patients with recent severe head trauma (within 3 mo), IV alteplase is contraindicated.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖’

condition: Acute head trauma during in-hospital phase leading to secondary AIS
recommendation: IV alteplase should not be administered for posttraumatic infarction during the acute in-hospital phase due to risk of exacerbating intracranial bleeding.
hint: In acute traumatic settings, thrombosis treatment risk is high.
original_text: ‘… IV alteplase should not be administered in posttraumatic infarction that occurs during the acute in-hospital phase.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖’

condition: Intracranial or intraspinal surgery within 3 months
recommendation: IV alteplase in AIS patients with recent intracranial or spinal surgery can be harmful and is generally contraindicated.
hint: Surgical sites may be at risk for rebleeding.
original_text: ‘For patients with AIS and a history of intracranial/spinal surgery within the prior 3 mo, IV alteplase is potentially harmful.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖’

condition: History of intracranial hemorrhage (ICH)
recommendation: IV alteplase is potentially harmful in AIS patients with a known history of intracranial hemorrhage; it is generally contraindicated.
hint: Increased risk of re-bleeding into damaged intracranial sites.
original_text: ‘IV alteplase administration … in patients who have a history of intracranial hemorrhage is potentially harmful.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖’

condition: Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)
recommendation: IV alteplase is contraindicated if clinical presentation strongly suggests SAH, even if initial CT is not definitive.
hint: Confirm no SAH with imaging (e.g., CTA, lumbar puncture) before considering IV alteplase.
original_text: ‘IV alteplase is contraindicated in patients presenting with symptoms and signs most consistent with an SAH.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖’

condition: Gastrointestinal (GI) malignancy or recent GI bleed (within 21 days)
recommendation: IV alteplase is potentially harmful in AIS patients with structural GI malignancy or a recent GI hemorrhage. High bleeding risk must be considered.
hint: Risk-benefit calculation is crucial where GI bleeding risk is elevated.
original_text: ‘Patients with a structural GI malignancy or recent bleeding event within 21 d … should be considered high risk, and IV alteplase administration is potentially harmful.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖’

condition: Coagulopathy (platelets <100,000/mm3, INR >1.7, aPTT >40s, PT >15s)
recommendation: IV alteplase is contraindicated or should be discontinued if these lab abnormalities are confirmed. Treatment can be started before labs return in patients without known risk, but must stop if results are out of range.
hint: Underlying coagulopathies significantly increase hemorrhage risk.
original_text: ‘The safety and efficacy … for acute stroke patients with platelets <100,000/mm3, INR >1.7, aPTT >40 s, or PT >15 s are unknown, and IV alteplase should not be administered.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖ … (In patients without history of thrombocytopenia, treatment … can be initiated before availability of platelet count … but discontinued if platelet count <100,000/mm3.)’

condition: Recent low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) use
recommendation: IV alteplase should not be administered to AIS patients who received a full treatment dose of LMWH within the previous 24 hours.
hint: Full-dose LMWH substantially increases hemorrhagic risk.
original_text: ‘IV alteplase should not be administered to patients who have received a full treatment dose of LMWH within the previous 24 h.† (COR III: Harm; LOE B-NR)§‡’

condition: Use of IV alteplase in patients taking direct thrombin inhibitors or factor Xa inhibitors
recommendation: IV alteplase is not firmly established and may be harmful in patients taking direct thrombin or factor Xa inhibitors except when labs (aPTT, INR, platelet count, ecarin clotting time, thrombin time, or direct factor Xa activity assays) are normal or the patient has not taken these agents for >48 hours (with normal renal function).
hint: Evaluate coagulation parameters or confirm that sufficient time (48 hours) has elapsed from last dose before considering IV alteplase.
original_text: “The use of IV alteplase in patients taking direct thrombin inhibitors or direct factor Xa inhibitors has not been firmly established but may be harmful.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖ IV alteplase should not be administered to patients taking direct thrombin inhibitors or direct factor Xa inhibitors unless laboratory tests such as aPTT, INR, platelet count, ecarin clotting time, thrombin time, or appropriate direct factor Xa activity assays are normal or the patient has not received a dose of these agents for >48 h (assuming normal renal metabolizing function).”

condition: Concomitant Abciximab use with IV alteplase
recommendation: Abciximab should not be administered concurrently with IV alteplase.
hint: Concomitant use increases bleeding risk—avoid combining these therapies.
original_text: “Abciximab should not be administered concurrently with IV alteplase. (COR III: Harm; LOE B-R)”

condition: Concomitant IV aspirin use with IV alteplase
recommendation: IV aspirin should not be administered within 90 minutes after the start of IV alteplase.
hint: Early concurrent administration may increase hemorrhagic risk.
original_text: “IV aspirin should not be administered within 90 min after the start of IV alteplase. (COR III: Harm; LOE B-R)”

condition: IV alteplase use in patients with infective endocarditis
recommendation: IV alteplase should not be administered to patients with acute ischemic stroke symptoms consistent with infective endocarditis because of increased intracranial hemorrhage risk.
hint: Infective endocarditis elevates hemorrhagic complications—avoid thrombolysis.
original_text: “For patients with AIS and symptoms consistent with infective endocarditis, treatment with IV alteplase should not be administered because of the increased risk of intracranial hemorrhage.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-LD)§‖”

condition: IV alteplase use in suspected aortic arch dissection
recommendation: IV alteplase should not be administered in AIS known or suspected to be associated with aortic arch dissection due to potential harm.
hint: Suspected aortic dissection is a contraindication—risk of catastrophic bleeding or extension of dissection.
original_text: “IV alteplase in AIS known or suspected to be associated with aortic arch dissection is potentially harmful and should not be administered.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖”

condition: IV alteplase use in intra-axial intracranial neoplasm
recommendation: IV alteplase treatment is potentially harmful for patients with AIS who have an intra-axial intracranial neoplasm.
hint: Risk of intracranial hemorrhage may be heightened with intracranial tumors—avoid IV alteplase.
original_text: “IV alteplase treatment for patients with AIS who harbor an intra-axial intracranial neoplasm is potentially harmful.† (COR III: Harm; LOE C-EO)§‖”

condition: Monitoring and management during/after IV alteplase infusion
recommendation: Perform neurological assessments and measure BP every 15 minutes during and for 2 hours after infusion, then every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly until 24 hours post-treatment. Discontinue infusion if severe headache, acute hypertension, nausea, vomiting, or neurologic worsening occurs, and obtain an emergency head CT.
hint: Strict neurological and BP monitoring is essential for early identification of hemorrhagic complications.
original_text: “Measure BP and perform neurological assessments every 15 min during and after IV alteplase infusion for 2 h, then every 30 min for 6 h, then hourly until 24 h after IV alteplase treatment. If the patient develops severe headache...obtain emergency head CT scan.” (Table 9)

condition: Use of tenecteplase in patients also eligible for mechanical thrombectomy
recommendation: It may be reasonable to choose tenecteplase (single IV bolus of 0.25 mg/kg, maximum 25 mg) over IV alteplase in patients without contraindications for IV fibrinolysis who are also eligible for mechanical thrombectomy.
hint: Supported by the EXTEND-IA TNK trial, which indicated that tenecteplase may be noninferior or possibly superior to alteplase in achieving early reperfusion.
original_text: 1. It may be reasonable to choose tenecteplase...over IV alteplase in patients without contraindications for IV fibrinolysis who are also eligible to undergo mechanical thrombectomy. (IIb; B-R)

condition: Tenecteplase for minor neurological impairment without major intracranial occlusion
recommendation: Tenecteplase administered as a 0.4-mg/kg single IV bolus has not been proven superior or noninferior to alteplase but might be considered as an alternative to alteplase in patients with minor neurological deficits and no major intracranial occlusion.
hint: In a large trial of predominantly mild strokes (median NIHSS score 4), tenecteplase failed to show superiority and had a similar safety profile to alteplase.
original_text: 2. Tenecteplase administered as a 0.4-mg/kg single IV bolus...might be considered as an alternative to alteplase in patients with minor neurological impairment and no major intracranial occlusion. (IIb; B-R)

condition: Administration of IV fibrinolytics other than alteplase and tenecteplase
recommendation: The administration of IV defibrinogenating agents or IV fibrinolytic agents other than alteplase and tenecteplase is not recommended.
hint: Randomized trials did not show benefit for streptokinase or desmoteplase across various time windows.
original_text: 3. The administration of IV defibrinogenating agents...other than alteplase and tenecteplase is not recommended. (III: No Benefit; B-R)

condition: Use of sonothrombolysis as adjuvant therapy with IV fibrinolysis
recommendation: Sonothrombolysis as an adjuvant to IV fibrinolysis is not recommended.
hint: Two RCTs (NOR-SASS and CLOTBUST-ER) showed no clinical benefit of sonothrombolysis when added to IV thrombolysis.
original_text: 4. The use of sonothrombolysis as adjuvant therapy with IV fibrinolysis is not recommended. (III: No Benefit; A)

condition: IV alteplase use in patients who may undergo mechanical thrombectomy
recommendation: Patients eligible for IV alteplase should receive IV alteplase even if mechanical thrombectomy is being considered.
hint: Continuing alteplase while preparing for thrombectomy has been recommended since earlier guidelines; evidence supports its use for improved functional outcomes.
original_text: 1. Patients eligible for IV alteplase should receive IV alteplase even if mechanical thrombectomy is being considered. (I; A)

condition: Concomitant IV Alteplase and Mechanical Thrombectomy
recommendation: In patients under consideration for mechanical thrombectomy, observation after IV alteplase to assess for clinical response should not be performed.
hint: Avoiding delays to mechanical thrombectomy is crucial because each hour of delay worsens functional outcomes.
original_text: “In patients under consideration for mechanical thrombectomy, observation after IV alteplase to assess for clinical response should not be performed… any cause for delay to mechanical thrombectomy, including observing for a clinical response after IV alteplase, should be avoided.”

condition: Mechanical Thrombectomy (0–6 Hours From Onset)
recommendation: Patients should receive mechanical thrombectomy with a stent retriever if they meet all of the following criteria: (1) prestroke mRS score of 0 to 1; (2) causative occlusion of the internal carotid artery or MCA segment 1 (M1); (3) age ≥18 years; (4) NIHSS score ≥6; (5) ASPECTS ≥6; and (6) treatment can be initiated (groin puncture) within 6 hours of symptom onset.
hint: These criteria derive from multiple high-level randomized trials supporting stent retrievers in acute large vessel occlusion.
original_text: “1. Patients should receive mechanical thrombectomy with a stent retriever if they meet all the following criteria: (1) prestroke mRS score of 0 to 1… (6) treatment can be initiated… within 6 hours of symptom onset.”

condition: Time to Reperfusion and Clinical Outcomes
recommendation: Shorter times to endovascular puncture and reperfusion are associated with better 90-day functional outcomes. Each 1-hour delay to substantial reperfusion is associated with worse disability (cOR, 0.84) and lower rates of functional independence (OR, 0.81), though mortality is not significantly changed.
hint: Statistical significance in improved outcome persists up to approximately 7 hours and 18 minutes from onset, emphasizing the need for prompt intervention.
evidence_level: Not explicitly stated in the recommendation (data drawn from a pooled meta-analysis).
recommended_level: Not explicitly stated in the recommendation (observational evidence).
source: 2023 AHA/ASA Stroke Guidelines, HERMES pooled analysis (Section 3.7.1)
original_text: “…the odds of better disability outcomes with the mechanical thrombectomy group declined with longer time from symptom onset to expected arterial puncture… cOR at 3 hours, 2.79… cOR at 6 hours, 1.98… cOR at 8 hours, 1.57… each 1-hour delay to reperfusion was associated with a less favorable degree of disability…”

condition: Patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) and large-vessel occlusion (LVO) in the internal carotid artery (ICA) or M1 segment, within 6 hours of onset, pre-stroke mRS score of 0–1, age ≥18, NIHSS score ≥6, and ASPECTS ≥6
recommendation: Direct aspiration thrombectomy as first-pass mechanical thrombectomy is recommended as noninferior to stent retriever for these patients when initiated (groin puncture) within 6 hours from symptom onset.
hint: Supported by COMPASS Trial results demonstrating noninferiority of direct aspiration versus stent retriever thrombectomy.
original_text: “2. Direct aspiration thrombectomy as first-pass mechanical thrombectomy is recommended as noninferior to stent retriever…within 6 hours of symptom onset.”

condition: Patients with acute ischemic stroke from M2 or M3 segment occlusions within 6 hours of onset
recommendation: Although the benefits are uncertain, the use of mechanical thrombectomy with stent retrievers may be reasonable for carefully selected patients with AIS and causative occlusion of M2 or M3 portions of the MCA.
hint: Pooled patient-level data (HERMES) showed a favorable direction of effect for M2 occlusions, though not statistically significant.
original_text: “3. Although the benefits are uncertain…mechanical thrombectomy with stent retrievers may be reasonable…MCA segment 2 (M2) or MCA segment 3 (M3).”

condition: Patients with AIS due to ICA or M1 occlusion who have one or more of the following: pre-stroke mRS >1, ASPECTS <6, or NIHSS <6, within 6 hours of onset
recommendation: Although the benefits are uncertain, mechanical thrombectomy with stent retrievers may be reasonable for these patients if treatment can be initiated (groin puncture) within 6 hours of symptom onset.
hint: 2015 Endovascular guidance remains unchanged; data are limited in patients with poor baseline functional status or borderline imaging findings.
original_text: “4. Although its benefits are uncertain…the use of mechanical thrombectomy with stent retrievers may be reasonable for…prestroke mRS score >1, ASPECTS <6, or NIHSS score <6…and ICA or proximal MCA (M1) occlusions.”

condition: Patients with AIS due to occlusion in anterior cerebral arteries, vertebral arteries, basilar artery, or posterior cerebral arteries within 6 hours of onset
recommendation: Although the benefits are uncertain, mechanical thrombectomy with stent retrievers may be reasonable for carefully selected patients in whom treatment can be initiated within 6 hours of symptom onset.
hint: Evidence is limited; recommendation reworded from 2015 Endovascular guidelines but COR remains unchanged.
original_text: “5. Although the benefits are uncertain…the use of mechanical thrombectomy with stent retrievers may be reasonable…for causative occlusion of the anterior cerebral arteries, vertebral arteries, basilar artery, or posterior cerebral arteries.”

condition: AIS (acute ischemic stroke) within 6 to 16 hours of last known normal (LVO in anterior circulation)
recommendation: Mechanical thrombectomy is recommended for selected patients who meet the DAWN or DEFUSE 3 eligibility criteria.
hint: These two trials used different imaging-based criteria to identify patients most likely to benefit; DAWN used clinical-core mismatch (NIHSS+CTP or DW-MRI), while DEFUSE 3 used perfusion-core mismatch and maximum core size.
original_text: "In selected patients with AIS within 6 to 16 hours of last known normal who have LVO in the anterior circulation and meet other DAWN or DEFUSE 3 eligibility criteria, mechanical thrombectomy is recommended. (COR I, LOE A)"

condition: AIS (acute ischemic stroke) within 16 to 24 hours of last known normal (LVO in anterior circulation)
recommendation: Mechanical thrombectomy is reasonable for selected patients who meet DAWN eligibility criteria.
hint: In the DAWN trial, patients showed functional benefit even if treated beyond 16 hours, provided imaging criteria were met.
original_text: "In selected patients with AIS within 16 to 24 hours of last known normal who have LVO in the anterior circulation and meet other DAWN eligibility criteria, mechanical thrombectomy is reasonable. (COR IIa, LOE B-R)"

condition: Device selection for endovascular mechanical thrombectomy in AIS
recommendation: Use of stent retrievers is indicated in preference to the MERCI device.
hint: Prior trials showed stent retrievers achieve higher recanalization rates and better outcomes than older-generation devices.
original_text: "Use of stent retrievers is indicated in preference to the Mechanical Embolus Removal in Cerebral Ischemia (MERCI) device. (COR I, LOE A)"

condition: Technical goal of mechanical thrombectomy in AIS
recommendation: The technical goal should be reperfusion to a modified Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction (mTICI) grade 2b/3 to maximize probability of good functional outcome.
hint: The mTICI grade 2b/3 threshold was used in all recent positive endovascular trials and correlates with better functional outcomes.
original_text: "The technical goal of the thrombectomy procedure should be reperfusion to a mTICI grade 2b/3 angiographic result to maximize the probability of a good functional clinical outcome. (COR I, LOE A)"

condition: Time to reperfusion during mechanical thrombectomy in AIS
recommendation: Ensure benefit by achieving mTICI 2b/3 reperfusion as early as possible within the therapeutic window.
hint: Data from patient-level meta-analyses (HERMES) show that for each hour of delay in achieving reperfusion, outcomes worsen significantly.
original_text: "To ensure benefit, reperfusion to mTICI grade 2b/3 should be achieved as early as possible within the therapeutic window. (COR I, LOE A)"

condition: Selection of anesthetic technique during endovascular therapy (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke (AIS)
recommendation: It is reasonable to select an anesthetic technique during EVT for AIS on the basis of individualized assessment of patient risk factors, technical performance of the procedure, and other clinical characteristics.
hint: Although retrospective data suggest general anesthesia might worsen outcomes, current prospective trial evidence is limited and does not show clear superiority of either technique. Either conscious sedation or general anesthesia is considered reasonable.
original_text: “5. It is reasonable to select an anesthetic technique during EVT for AIS on the basis of individualized assessment of patient risk factors, technical performance of the procedure, and other clinical characteristics… All failed to show superiority of GA for the primary end point… either method of procedural sedation for acute stroke endovascular procedures is reasonable.”

condition: Catheter choice for stent retriever-based endovascular therapy
recommendation: The use of a proximal balloon guide catheter or a large-bore distal-access catheter, rather than a cervical guide catheter alone, in conjunction with stent retrievers may be beneficial.
hint: Using a balloon guide catheter or large-bore distal-access catheter can potentially improve clot retrieval efficiency and reduce distal embolization, but direct comparative data remain limited.
original_text: “6. The use of a proximal balloon guide catheter or a large-bore distal-access catheter, rather than a cervical guide catheter alone, in conjunction with stent retrievers may be beneficial. Recommendation and COR unchanged from 2015 Endovascular…”

condition: Treatment of tandem occlusions (extracranial and intracranial) with mechanical thrombectomy
recommendation: Treatment of tandem occlusions when performing mechanical thrombectomy may be reasonable.
hint: Recent trials included tandem lesions, with variable methods (e.g., no revascularization vs. angioplasty vs. stenting) at the extracranial site. Overall, mechanical thrombectomy improves outcomes, but the optimal approach for tandem occlusions is not yet clearly defined.
original_text: “7. Treatment of tandem occlusions (both extracranial and intracranial occlusions)… In HERMES, there is heterogeneity of treatment methods… No conclusions about the optimum treatment approach for patients with tandem occlusions are therefore possible.”

condition: Use of IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors during endovascular stroke treatment
recommendation: The safety and efficacy of IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors administered during endovascular stroke treatment are uncertain.
hint: Current literature is mostly retrospective or limited to case series; large-scale, multi-center trials are needed to determine whether peri-procedural glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor use is beneficial or harmful.
original_text: “8. The safety and efficacy of IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors administered during endovascular stroke treatment are uncertain… The published literature is limited primarily to case series and retrospective reviews…”

condition: Salvage technical adjuncts (including intra-arterial fibrinolysis) in mechanical thrombectomy
recommendation: Use of salvage technical adjuncts, including intra-arterial fibrinolysis, may be reasonable to achieve mTICI grade 2b/3 angiographic results.
hint: Intra-arterial fibrinolysis is typically used as a rescue strategy after stent retriever attempts. Available trial data show no clear advantage or harm, but usage rates have been relatively low. Further research is needed.
original_text: “9. Use of salvage technical adjuncts, including intra-arterial fibrinolysis, may be reasonable to achieve mTICI grade 2b/3 angiographic results… In THRACE, an intra-arterial lytic was used… There was no effect on outcomes compared with mechanical thrombectomy alone.”

condition: Blood Pressure Management in Mechanical Thrombectomy
recommendation: In patients who undergo mechanical thrombectomy, it is reasonable to maintain the BP at ≤180/105 mm Hg during and for 24 hours after the procedure.
hint: RCT data on optimal BP management in this setting are currently lacking; this recommendation is based on limited observational evidence and expert consensus.
original_text: 1. In patients who undergo mechanical thrombectomy, it is reasonable to maintain the BP at ≤180/105 mm Hg during and for 24 hours after the procedure. (COR IIa, LOE B-NR; New recommendation.)

condition: Blood Pressure Management After Successful Reperfusion in Mechanical Thrombectomy
recommendation: In patients who undergo mechanical thrombectomy with successful reperfusion, it might be reasonable to maintain BP at a level <180/105 mm Hg.
hint: This recommendation acknowledges that once restoration of blood flow is achieved, a lower BP target may reduce the risk of intracranial hemorrhage, though supporting data remain sparse.
original_text: 2. In patients who undergo mechanical thrombectomy with successful reperfusion, it might be reasonable to maintain BP at a level <180/105 mm Hg. (COR IIb, LOE B-NR; New recommendation.)

condition: First-Line Mechanical Thrombectomy Versus Intra-Arterial Fibrinolysis
recommendation: Mechanical thrombectomy with stent retrievers is recommended over intra-arterial fibrinolysis as first-line therapy.
hint: Evidence from multiple trials supports stent retrievers as more effective than intra-arterial fibrinolysis alone in improving outcomes for large-vessel occlusion strokes.
original_text: 1. Mechanical thrombectomy with stent retrievers is recommended over intra-arterial fibrinolysis as first-line therapy. (COR I, LOE C-EO.)

condition: Intra-Arterial Fibrinolysis for Stroke Patients with IV Alteplase Contraindications
recommendation: Intra-arterial fibrinolysis initiated within 6 hours of stroke onset in carefully selected patients who have contraindications to the use of IV alteplase might be considered, but the consequences are unknown.
hint: This option may be relevant when intravenous alteplase cannot be administered; clinical data on efficacy and safety remain limited.
original_text: 2. Intra-arterial fibrinolysis initiated within 6 hours of stroke onset in carefully selected patients who have contraindications to the use of IV alteplase might be considered, but the consequences are unknown. (COR IIb, LOE C-EO.)

condition: Antiplatelet Treatment in Acute Ischemic Stroke
recommendation: Administration of aspirin is recommended in patients with AIS within 24 to 48 hours after onset. For those treated with IV alteplase, aspirin administration is generally delayed until 24 hours later.
hint: Aspirin dosage in supporting trials ranged between 160 and 300 mg. Early administration can reduce stroke recurrence and mortality.
original_text: 1. Administration of aspirin is recommended in patients with AIS within 24 to 48 hours after onset ... COR I, LOE A. Recommendation revised from 2013 AIS Guidelines.

condition: Minor noncardioembolic ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤3) without IV alteplase treatment
recommendation: Initiate dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) within 24 hours of onset and continue for 21 days to reduce recurrent stroke up to 90 days.
hint: Both CHANCE and POINT trials showed the greatest benefit within the first 30 days of treatment, though the risk of bleeding was higher after the first week. This is a new Class I recommendation with Level A evidence.
source: AHA/ASA 2019 AIS Guidelines, Section 3.9 - Antiplatelet Treatment
original_text: “2. In patients presenting with minor noncardioembolic ischemic stroke (NIHSS score ≤3) who did not receive IV alteplase, treatment with dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel) started within 24 hours after symptom onset and continued for 21 days is effective ... COR I, LOE A, New recommendation.”

condition: Use of IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (tirofiban, eptifibatide) in acute ischemic stroke
recommendation: Their efficacy in AIS is not well established, and they should be used cautiously, if at all, outside of clinical trials.
hint: Phase II trials suggest safety, but more RCTs are needed to confirm efficacy. Previously revised from 2013 AIS Guidelines.
source: AHA/ASA 2019 AIS Guidelines, Section 3.9 - Antiplatelet Treatment
original_text: “3. The efficacy of the IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors tirofiban and eptifibatide in the treatment of AIS is not well established. COR IIb, LOE B-R, Recommendation revised from 2013 AIS Guidelines.”

condition: Minor acute ischemic stroke management with ticagrelor versus aspirin
recommendation: Ticagrelor is not recommended over aspirin for patients with minor acute stroke.
hint: The SOCRATES trial did not demonstrate superiority of ticagrelor over aspirin for preventing stroke, MI, or death up to 90 days. Ticagrelor may still be considered if aspirin is contraindicated.
source: AHA/ASA 2019 AIS Guidelines, Section 3.9 - Antiplatelet Treatment
original_text: “4. Ticagrelor is not recommended over aspirin for treatment of patients with minor acute stroke. COR III: No Benefit, LOE B-R, New recommendation.”

condition: Use of IV abciximab for acute ischemic stroke
recommendation: IV abciximab is potentially harmful and should not be used to treat AIS.
hint: A Cochrane review and the AbESTT phase III trial showed a significant risk of intracranial hemorrhage without improvement in death or disability outcomes. Recommendation revised from 2013 AIS Guidelines.
source: AHA/ASA 2019 AIS Guidelines, Section 3.9 - Antiplatelet Treatment
original_text: “5. The administration of the IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor abciximab as medical treatment for AIS is potentially harmful and should not be performed. COR III: Harm, LOE B-R.”

condition: Use of aspirin instead of IV alteplase or mechanical thrombectomy in eligible patients
recommendation: Aspirin is not recommended as a substitute for acute stroke treatment in patients otherwise eligible for IV alteplase or mechanical thrombectomy.
hint: Aspirin alone does not provide the same benefit as IV alteplase or mechanical thrombectomy in acute ischemic stroke and is considered a harmful alternative in that setting.
source: AHA/ASA 2019 AIS Guidelines, Section 3.9 - Antiplatelet Treatment
category: Acute Ischemic Stroke / Acute Reperfusion Strategies
original_text: “6. Aspirin is not recommended as a substitute for acute stroke treatment in patients who are otherwise eligible for IV alteplase or mechanical thrombectomy. COR III: Harm, LOE B-R.”

condition: Urgent anticoagulation in patients with severe internal carotid artery stenosis after acute ischemic stroke (AIS)
recommendation: The usefulness of urgent anticoagulation in patients with severe stenosis of an internal carotid artery ipsilateral to an ischemic stroke is not well established.
hint: Although this approach remains an option (COR IIb), its overall benefit is uncertain (LOE B-NR). Further research may clarify its utility.
original_text: 1. The usefulness of urgent anticoagulation in patients with severe stenosis of an internal carotid artery ipsilateral to an ischemic stroke is not well established. (IIb, B-NR). Recommendation and COR unchanged from 2013 AIS Guidelines. LOE amended to conform with ACC/AHA 2015 Recommendation Classification System.

condition: Short-term anticoagulation for nonocclusive, extracranial intraluminal thrombus in AIS
recommendation: The safety and usefulness of short-term anticoagulation for nonocclusive, extracranial intraluminal thrombus in the setting of AIS are not well established.
hint: Small observational studies suggest potential safety, but evidence is limited. Further research is needed to determine benefits and risks.
original_text: 2. The safety and usefulness of short-term anticoagulation for nonocclusive, extracranial intraluminal thrombus in the setting of AIS are not well established. (IIb, C-LD). New recommendation.

condition: Use of thrombin inhibitors (argatroban, dabigatran) for AIS treatment
recommendation: At present, the usefulness of argatroban, dabigatran, or other thrombin inhibitors for the treatment of patients with AIS is not well established.
hint: Preliminary observational studies show feasibility and safety, including adjunctive uses with alteplase, but further clinical trials are required to confirm effectiveness.
original_text: 3. At present, the usefulness of argatroban, dabigatran, or other thrombin inhibitors for the treatment of patients with AIS is not well established. (IIb, B-R). Recommendation revised from 2013 AIS Guidelines.

condition: Oral factor Xa inhibitors in AIS treatment
recommendation: The safety and usefulness of oral factor Xa inhibitors in the treatment of AIS are not well established.
hint: Evidence on factor Xa inhibitors (e.g., rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) for acute stroke is limited to small studies and ongoing trials.
original_text: 4. The safety and usefulness of oral factor Xa inhibitors in the treatment of AIS are not well established. (IIb, C-LD). New recommendation.

condition: Urgent anticoagulation to prevent early recurrence, halt neurological worsening, or improve outcomes after AIS
recommendation: Urgent anticoagulation, with the goal of preventing early recurrent stroke, halting neurological worsening, or improving outcomes after AIS, is not recommended for treatment of patients with AIS.
hint: Meta-analyses confirm no benefit from urgent anticoagulation in this population. LMWH vs. aspirin also showed no differences in long-term functional outcomes.
original_text: 5. Urgent anticoagulation, with the goal of preventing early recurrent stroke, halting neurological worsening, or improving outcomes after AIS, is not recommended for treatment of patients with AIS. (III: No Benefit, A).

condition: Hemodilution (volume expansion) therapy for AIS
recommendation: Hemodilution by volume expansion is not recommended for treatment of patients with AIS.
hint: Multiple RCTs indicate no lasting benefit from hemodilution therapy in acute ischemic stroke, confirming previous guideline statements.
original_text: 1. Hemodilution by volume expansion is not recommended for treatment of patients with AIS. (III: No Benefit, A). Recommendation and LOE unchanged from 2013 AIS Guidelines.

condition: High-dose albumin therapy for AIS
recommendation: The administration of high-dose albumin is not recommended for the treatment of patients with AIS.
hint: The ALIAS trials revealed no significant difference in 90-day disability outcomes, leading to early study termination for futility.
original_text: 2. The administration of high-dose albumin is not recommended for the treatment of patients with AIS. (III: No Benefit, A). Recommendation revised from 2013 AIS Guidelines.

condition: Use of vasodilatory agents in acute ischemic stroke (AIS)
recommendation: The administration of vasodilatory agents, such as pentoxifylline, is not recommended for treatment of patients with AIS.
hint: No evidence of benefit in AIS management; recommendation unchanged from 2013 AIS Guidelines.
original_text: 3. The administration of vasodilatory agents, such as pentoxifylline, is not recommended for treatment of patients with AIS. (III: No Benefit, LOE=A). Recommendation and LOE unchanged from 2013 AIS Guidelines. COR amended to conform with ACC/AHA 2015 Recommendation Classification System.

condition: Use of mechanical devices to augment cerebral blood flow in AIS
recommendation: Devices to mechanically augment cerebral blood flow for the treatment of patients with AIS are not useful.
hint: No proven benefit; a feasibility RCT of external counterpulsation showed no significant improvement in outcomes.
original_text: 4. Devices to mechanically augment cerebral blood flow for the treatment of patients with AIS are not useful. (III: No Benefit, B-R). New recommendation.

condition: Pharmacological or nonpharmacological neuroprotective therapies in AIS
recommendation: At present, pharmacological or nonpharmacological treatments with putative neuroprotective actions are not recommended.
hint: Trials such as FAST-MAG and ALIAS have not shown benefit; recommendation reworded from 2013 but unchanged in substance.
original_text: 1. At present, pharmacological or nonpharmacological treatments with putative neuroprotective actions are not recommended. (III: No Benefit, A). Recommendation reworded for clarity from 2013 AIS Guidelines. LOE unchanged. COR amended to conform with ACC/AHA 2015 Recommendation Classification System.

condition: Emergency or urgent carotid endarterectomy/carotid angioplasty and stenting for AIS with small infarct core but large territory at risk
recommendation: The usefulness of emergent or urgent carotid endarterectomy (CEA) and carotid angioplasty/stenting is not well established in these patients.
hint: Limited evidence supports or refutes the procedure in select patients with compromised flow due to critical carotid stenosis/occlusion.
original_text: 1. The usefulness of emergent or urgent CEA/carotid angioplasty and stenting... is not well established. (IIb, B-NR). Recommendation reworded for clarity from 2013 AIS Guidelines. COR unchanged. LOE amended to conform with the ACC/AHA 2015 Recommendation Classification System.

condition: Emergency or urgent CEA/carotid angioplasty and stenting in patients with unstable neurological status
recommendation: In patients with unstable neurological status (stroke-in-evolution), the efficacy of emergency or urgent CEA/carotid angioplasty and stenting is not well established.
hint: No clear evidence to support urgent revascularization in evolving clinical presentations.
original_text: 2. In patients with unstable neurological status (eg, stroke-in-evolution), the efficacy of emergency or urgent CEA/carotid angioplasty and stenting is not well established. (IIb, B-NR). Recommendation reworded for clarity from 2013 AIS Guidelines. COR unchanged. LOE amended to conform with ACC/AHA 2015 Recommendation Classification System.

condition: Transcranial near-infrared laser therapy for AIS
recommendation: Transcranial near-infrared laser therapy is not recommended for the treatment of AIS.
hint: NEST-3 trial showed futility compared to sham treatment and no evidence of clinical benefit.
original_text: 1. Transcranial near-infrared laser therapy is not recommended for the treatment of AIS. (III: No Benefit, B-R). Recommendation revised from 2013 AIS Guidelines. Study NEST-3 was terminated for futility.
